options: Speed with a direction, such as 80 km/h east
The total distance traveled per hour
A push or pull on an object
How heavy an object is
questions.explanation: Velocity joins a speed with a direction — it tells both how fast and which way. Distance per hour without a direction is speed only.
questions.misconception: Some think velocity and speed are synonyms. The whole point of the component is the direction slapping the two apart.

questions.prompt: Why is velocity called a vector quantity?
options: Because it has both magnitude and direction
Because it only has one big number
Because it has no direction at all
Because it is always measured in meters
questions.explanation: A vector always carries both size and direction — like an arrow. Velocity's direction is as real as its number, so up arrows draw velocity best.
questions.misconception: Learners mix 'vector' up with 'big' or 'powerful'; it's a word for direction-carryingness, not for size.

questions.prompt: A car drives a perfect circle at a constant 20 m/s. Which is true?
options: The speed is constant but the velocity is always changing
The velocity is constant but the speed changes
Both speed and velocity are constant
Both speed and velocity keep changing
questions.explanation: On the circle the arrow always turns to point along the road, so the direction part — and hence velocity — keeps changing while the 20 m/s size holds.
questions.misconception: The intuition 'constant speed = same motion' is exactly wrong: the turning is a real change in velocity, not a mood buzz about the speedometer.

questions.prompt: On a position-time graph, what does a downward-slanting line describe?
options: Negative velocity — the object is moving back toward the start
The object standing still
Speeding up quickly
The object being dropped
questions.explanation: A position sliding back down means displacement is decreasing, so velocity is negative — the direction has reversed to 'back toward home.'
questions.misconception: Downward isn't 'falling' or 'slowing'; it's motion in the reverse direction on the graph's scale.

options: displacement ÷ time
distance ÷ time
mass × speed
distance + time
questions.explanation: Velocity = displacement ÷ time, not distance ÷ time. Displacement brings the direction, so velocity keeps its arrow.
questions.misconception: distance ÷ time (the speed answer) is the sleeper wrong choice — the direction-holding displacement is the bit that turns speed into velocity.
